common_name: Salcedo INIA Quinoa (Peru's Most Widely Grown Commercial Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct-sow around the last frost date; this high-altitude Puno line matures fastest and yields heaviest when grown in warmer valley or near-sea-level conditions rather than cold highland climates.

directions: Salcedo INIA was bred from a 1983 cross of the Real Boliviana and Sajama varieties at INIA's Illpa Puno station and formally released to Puno-region growers in 1995, making it one of the oldest INIA quinoa releases still in wide commercial use. Its sweet, low-saponin, cream-white grain and strong adaptability have made it the most widely planted improved quinoa variety in Peru, with especially high yields when grown in interandean valleys or on the coast rather than its native highland environment. The plant carries a compact white panicle atop stems that reach 1.5 to 1.7 meters, maturing in about 150 days at altitude but considerably faster in warmer valley and coastal plantings. Because the grain requires minimal rinsing to remove bitterness, Salcedo INIA is a favorite for home-scale processing into pearled, laminated, or ground quinoa products.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

common_name: Illpa INIA Quinoa (Puno High-Yield White Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring and allow a long, cool season; this tall, high-altitude Puno line needs the full growing window to fill its sizeable grain heads.

directions: Illpa INIA was released in 1997 by INIA's Illpa Puno experimental station from a cross of the Sajama and Juli Blanca varieties, with selection work carried out at the Salcedo annex beginning in 1985. It grows into one of the tallest commercial quinoa types, reaching 1.5 to 1.8 meters, and bears a compact white panicle filled with large, cream-white, very low-saponin grain prized for pearling, flour, and semolina. Adapted to the cold, semi-dry lakeshore and suni zones of the Puno highlands, it is a dependable yielder that remains one of the parent lines behind several newer INIA releases. Direct-sow in full sun on well-drained soil and give it the long highland season it needs to fill out its grain heads fully.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

common_name: INIA 431 - Altiplano Quinoa (Illpa x Salcedo Cross, Puno Release)

planting.note: Direct-sow around the last frost date; this 2013 Puno release has since also been successfully trialed on Peru's coast, where it finishes faster than at altitude.

directions: INIA 431 - Altiplano is a 2013 release from Peru's National Institute of Agricultural Innovation (INIA) at its Illpa Puno experimental station, produced by reciprocal crosses between the earlier Illpa INIA and Salcedo INIA varieties. It forms a tall, unbranched plant with a green, amaranth-shaped panicle that turns white at maturity and yields cream-white, low-saponin grain requiring only light rinsing before cooking. Bred for the cold, semi-dry Puno altiplano around Lake Titicaca, it tolerates light frost and brief drought better than many commercial lines, and it has since also been grown successfully on Peru's coast. Grow it exactly as other quinoa: direct-sow into well-drained soil in full sun and let the plant finish its full season before the grain heads are cut and threshed.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

planting.note: Direct-sow after the last frost; Pasankalla is unusually flexible across elevations and finishes notably faster when grown at low elevation or on the coast than in the Puno highlands.

directions: INIA 415 - Pasankalla was released by INIA's Illpa Puno station in 2006 following panicle-groove selection from a germplasm bank accession collected in Caritamaya, Acora District, in 1978. Its signature feature is a vivid pink-to-wine-colored panicle that, combined with its sweet, essentially saponin-free grain, has made it one of the best-known Peruvian quinoas marketed internationally as 'red quinoa.' Pasankalla is unusually adaptable for a Puno-bred line, performing in the cold highland altiplano as well as in interandean valleys and even on the Peruvian coast at low elevation. Traditionally it is also baked into k'ispiño bread rolls in addition to the usual soups, stews, and toasted or expanded grain preparations.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

common_name: INIA 420 - Black Collana Quinoa (Peruvian Shiny Black Grain Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct-sow around the last frost date; this is one of the fastest-maturing INIA quinoa releases, well suited to shorter growing seasons.

directions: INIA 420 - Black Collana was released by INIA's Illpa Puno station in 2008 from thirteen landrace accessions gathered in 1978 from the Caritamaya area of Acora District, long known locally as 'Quytu jiwras.' The compact, unbranched plants produce a grey, glomerulate panicle filled with small, shiny jet-black grain that carries essentially no saponin, so it needs little rinsing before cooking. It is one of the fastest-maturing varieties in INIA's commercial lineup, reaching physiological maturity in as little as 138 days in the highlands or 115 days in interandean valleys, and it tolerates both cold and drought well. Market demand for dark-grained quinoa has made Black Collana a popular choice for flour, expanded snacks, and striking black-and-white grain blends.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

common_name: INIA 427 - Yellow Sacaca Quinoa (Cusco Valley Bitter Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct-sow after frost risk has passed; this Cusco valley variety is sensitive to cold snaps and needs a long, mild season of 160 days or more to finish.

directions: INIA 427 - Yellow Sacaca was released by INIA's Andenes Experimental Station in Cusco in 2011, derived from panicle-groove selection of traditional quinoa collected from the Sacaca community in Calca Province back in 1994. Its branching plants carry orange-flowering, amaranth-shaped panicles that mature into a striking golden-orange seed head, producing yellow grain with a notably high saponin content that must be thoroughly washed or processed before eating. It is best suited to the interandean valley floors of Cusco and Apurímac between roughly 2,750 and 3,650 meters elevation and is sensitive to cold snaps, so valley gardeners should avoid overly exposed planting sites. The variety carries one of the longer quinoa cycles in INIA's catalogue, needing 160 to 170 days to reach full physiological maturity.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

common_name: Quillahuaman INIA Quinoa (Cusco Vilcanota Valley Quinoa)

planting.note: Direct-sow once frost danger is past; this long-season Cusco valley heirloom-derived variety needs up to 200 days to mature and is more vulnerable to cold and mildew than Puno-bred highland lines.

directions: Quillahuaman INIA was released in 1990 by INIA's Andenes Experimental Station in Cusco from mass selection of traditional quinoa growing in the Vilcanota Valley. It is a tall, heavily branched plant that needs a long 180- to 200-day season to finish, considerably longer than most other INIA releases, and its cream-colored grain carries a moderate saponin level that calls for thorough washing before cooking. The variety is suited only to interandean valley floors up to about 3,500 meters in Cusco and Apurímac, since it is notably more vulnerable to cold snaps and mildew than Puno-bred highland varieties. Its long history of cultivation in the Vilcanota Valley makes it one of the more traditional selections among Peru's named commercial quinoa varieties.
sources: FAO and INIA, Catalogue of Commercial Varieties of Quinoa in Peru (FAO/INIA, Lima, 2015)

common_name: Canchán Potato (INIA 303, Peru's Leading Late-Blight-Resistant Variety)

planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost; Canchán has a notably long vegetative period and sprawling habit, so it needs a full, long growing season to bulk up tubers.

directions: Canchán, officially registered as INIA 303 - Canchán, was released nationally in 1990 from the INIA experimental station of the same name in Huánuco, the product of a joint breeding program between Peru's International Potato Center (CIP) and INIA. Bred specifically for durable resistance to late blight (rancha), the disease that historically devastated Andean potato crops, it quickly became Peru's most widely grown variety, still covering a large share of the country's potato area decades after release. The plant has a long vegetative period and a sprawling, decumbent habit with intense purple flowers, and its tubers have red skin over pale-yellow, high-dry-matter flesh suited equally to boiling, baking, chipping, and french fries. On-farm yields more than double Peru's national potato average helped make Canchán an unusually fast-payback success story for INIA's breeding program.
sources: INIA Peru — Papa INIA 303 - Canchán variety technical bulletin
